BT Group plc (BT.A-GB): the end of the fibre build is turning BT's earnings into cash, but the shares already price that improvement, so the return depends on the multiple

Written 24 November 2026 for Richard. Share price 215.8p at 13 November 2026. BT's fiscal year ends on 31 March, so FY27 is the year to March 2027. Money is in pounds sterling and per-share figures are in pence; definitions are in the end notes.

SummarySummary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in brief. BT has finished the expensive part of building its national fibre network. Capital expenditure now falls by about a third, and because BT owns the network, the saving arrives as cash. In October and November 2026 the three external threats to that cash eased together (#1), and BT settled its pension valuation early. BT's business case is stronger than at any point in the last 18 months. The share price already reflects that improvement: the shares rose about 18% into the half-year results, fell after the results beat expectations, and now stand at the 82nd percentile of their own ten-year valuation range. The business is predictable and improving; the return from here depends on the multiple the market pays.

Six insights that matter most

  1. The end of the build reaches cash years before it reaches earnings. The end of the build cuts capital expenditure now, but the assets already built stay in the depreciation charge into the 2030s. Normalised free cash flow therefore grows about 16% a year from FY27 to FY30, while EPS grows 6% to 7% a year. The step-up from FY27 to FY30 is a step-up in cash. The step-up in earnings comes later, in FY31 to FY33, when buybacks start, pension cash payments fall by about £490m a year and build-era assets begin to drop out of the depreciation charge.
  2. The quality of BT's earnings is changing more than their quantity. In FY26 each pound of adjusted net income produced 23p of cash that shareholders could claim. On the model's path, that figure rises to about 95p by FY30, and reported EPS converges on adjusted EPS. This improving cash conversion is the strongest argument that BT's historical multiple range understates what its earnings are now worth.
  3. The model sits on consensus for earnings and above consensus for cash. The model's group EPS is within 3.5% of consensus in every year. The model's normalised free cash flow is about £0.2bn above consensus in FY29 and £0.5bn above in FY30. The scope for upgrades therefore lies in cash estimates and capital-expenditure guidance, with little scope in EPS.
  4. Unfavourable news comes first and favourable news later. Between February and May 2027, several items will read badly without changing BT's economics: about £2.4bn of pension notes entering reported net debt, TalkTalk's losses entering estimates, and the depreciation charge disappointing the most bullish brokers. From May 2027 the favourable items arrive: a first guide for revenue growth, capital expenditure guided below estimates, and reported net debt falling by more than £1bn a year.
  5. Management meets its guidance and does not raise it. Management reconfirmed guidance after a 3.2% EBITDA beat. Good news therefore arrives as delivery at the two main results dates each year, and seldom as a raised guide between them.
  6. The return depends on the multiple. At Viewforth's guideline fair multiple of 7.25 times, the model's return to March 2028 is -18.5%. At an unchanged multiple of 10.9 times, the return is about +19%, and the return is nil at about 9.1 times. Each turn of the multiple is worth about 10 points of return, while the whole plausible range of FY28 EPS is worth about 8 points.
Against Richard's test. BT's fundamental outcomes are narrow and dependable, but the probability of upgrades to guidance and to sell-side estimates is not unusually skewed to the positive today. For EPS, that probability leans slightly negative over the next six months. The skew can turn favourable after the May 2027 results, once the presentational negatives are in the numbers and cash estimates start to rise, and more so if the multiple has fallen by then.

Five judgements move the shares most (the arithmetic is in #9): whether the second half of FY27 delivers the cash and capital expenditure keeps falling; whether core EBITDA grows about 1% a year; how depreciation and the interest on the pension notes are reported; whether Openreach's line losses keep falling; and how the TalkTalk review ends. The multiple (#11 and #12) matters more than all five.

Where I differ from the market. I side with the bulls on operations and cash, and with consensus against the bulls on depreciation. I therefore expect EPS growth of 6% to 7% a year, where the most bullish broker has about 11%. I think the bears are too cautious on line losses and on FY29 to FY30 cash. I think both sides misdate two events: the fall in pension cash payments (FY32, which some read as FY28) and the first buyback (FY31, where some hope for news in May 2027).

1Tailwinds and headwinds: the wholesale layer turned favourable in autumn 2026, while retail competition and gilt yields still push against BT

Conclusion. BT's operating environment turned clearly favourable at the wholesale layer in autumn 2026. Retail competition and gilt yields remain real headwinds, so BT has a strong tailwind with headwinds still present, not a tailwind without headwinds.

Evidence

  • Wholesale, where the value sits. Openreach earns about 55% of core EBITDA, and four developments in two months favour it. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) provisionally found against nexfibre's purchase of Netomnia; its final decision is due by 15 December 2026, and no remedies have been offered. Virgin Media O2, at 5.7 times leverage, halted its fibre upgrade and is discussing renting Openreach's network in rural areas. Alternative-network build is down at least 40%. TalkTalk, which Morgan Stanley identifies as the source of more than half of Openreach's line losses, is now owned by BT. Openreach's quarterly line losses have fallen from 203,000 to 192,000 to 175,000.
  • Regulation. Ofcom's final decision of 28 September 2026 blocked one Openreach discount, approved two other Openreach offers and set no cap on margin squeeze. Ofcom's regulatory framework runs to 2031.
  • Demand. UK broadband lines have been flat at 28.6m for four years. The one dated change is the switch-off of the old telephone network on 31 January 2027, which ends a legacy-voice drag of £150m to £200m a year, about one point of service revenue.
  • Retail. Retail competition is intensifying. Consumer broadband revenue per user fell 3% in the first half and net additions turned negative, under pressure from alternative networks, low-priced mobile brands, VodafoneThree's push into fixed wireless and Starlink at £32 a month.
  • Costs and rates. Labour, BT's dominant cost, is inflating, and energy hedging falls from 88% of FY27 needs to 52% of FY28 needs. The ten-year gilt yields about 5.3%, and the telecoms sector's multiple fell 12% from May to September 2026 while estimates held.

Inference. The tailwinds are concentrated where BT earns most, and the headwinds sit at retail and in the discount rate. One cause links the two: capital is scarce and dear. Scarce, dear capital starves BT's wholesale challengers and compresses BT's multiple at the same time. The case therefore carries a partial internal hedge: the high yields that hurt BT's share price also protect Openreach's volumes.

So what. Three assumptions are reasonable: line losses below the guided path, service revenue moving from -1% to slightly positive in FY28, and flat Consumer profit. The environment supports the cash case; it does not support a growth case.
Counter-case. The wholesale threat has been delayed and reshaped, not removed. CityFibre is recapitalising and is reported to be in talks to buy Netomnia, which would create an independent wholesaler covering about 8m premises. Sky already buys from CityFibre, and Redburn puts 450,000 to 650,000 Openreach lines at risk from that supply agreement. Alternative networks pass about 20m premises at about 16% take-up, so they can keep taking lines for years without building more. Management also kept its guide of about 800,000 line losses a month after taking ownership of TalkTalk.

What would change my view. Quarterly line losses back above 200,000; a cleared CityFibre-Netomnia deal followed by Sky moving volume to CityFibre; Consumer EBITDA falling where management expects it to be flat.

Against the market. I agree with the bullish brokers that wholesale risk has passed its peak. I think the bearish brokers' FY27 line losses of 800,000 are too high; the model has 720,000. No broker publishes an FY28 view; the model has 550,000, and I think 650,000 is as likely, a difference that matters more to the narrative than to earnings. The market underweights one implication of a CMA block on nexfibre: the block points to CityFibre as the consolidator.

Score: 59, set by the Rater. The environment is a real, structural net positive where BT earns most. Openreach (about 55% of core EBITDA) gains from capital-starved challengers (alternative-network build down 40% or more, Virgin Media O2 halting its upgrade, the CMA against nexfibre), from Ofcom's framework to 2031 and from the end of a £150m to £200m voice drag, and its line losses have fallen from 203,000 to 175,000 a quarter. The positive is offset by intensifying retail competition (broadband revenue per user down 3%, negative net additions), labour and energy cost inflation and a CityFibre consolidator, and it only moves service revenue from about -1% to slightly positive (consensus sales growth at the 8th percentile). The result is a clear but modest positive, a little above the group's 56 because wholesale price indexation counts as well as volume; the TalkTalk purchase is counted in topic 2.

2Internally driven corporate change: a broad, funded reset that lands in cash, not in revenue

Conclusion. Corporate change at BT is strong, broad and well resourced, and it has just removed two tail risks. Its limits are that it produces cash on a flat revenue line and that BT's commercial execution is still to be proven.

Evidence

  • Leadership. BT's chief executive (since February 2024), its chief financial officer (since September 2026, from Virgin Media O2) and Openreach's chief executive (since April 2026) are all new, and all three stand behind one programme: UK only, cost out, capital expenditure down, cash up, then distributions.
  • Capital and cost. The build peak passed on schedule. BT has delivered £1.7bn of a £3.5bn gross savings target. Total labour fell 11% in a year to 90,000, and in November management cut the FY30 labour target to 65,000 to 70,000.
  • Perimeter. Five international disposals are complete, and the International unit goes into a joint venture with Verizon in the second half of 2027, bringing $625m.
  • Two actions since September that remove tail risks. BT bought TalkTalk out of administration for a total FY27 cash cost of about £400m, protecting about £1bn a year of Openreach revenue. BT also settled the pension valuation early: the deficit fell from £3.7bn to £2.7bn, and the agreement permits distributions of up to £1.5bn in FY27, rising to £2.0bn by FY30.
  • Problems. First-half normalised free cash flow was £236m, and net debt rose £1.04bn. Business EBITDA fell 7%. The 25m-premise build target slipped three months, and unit build cost drifted up within its range. Restructuring cost per paid leaver rose from about £67,000 to about £159,000. Five top roles changed in eighteen months, and the General Counsel is retiring during the CMA review.

Inference. BT's management adapts when a lever is blocked. When Ofcom stopped it defending the wholesale base with price, management defended the base through ownership of TalkTalk. When the pension was a risk, management settled the valuation a year early and obtained permission to distribute. The change programme is broad and resourced, and it lands in capital expenditure, cost and cash. It does not land in revenue.

So what. Give high weight to what management controls and guides: cost, capital expenditure and the cash target. Give low weight to commercial improvement, where management's FY26 scorecard paid nothing on three measures.
Counter-case. The labour target requires cuts of about 8% a year for three and a half more years. The research found no incumbent that cut a quarter of its labour in under four years with stable service, and BT has done one such year. If exits must be paid for at the FY26 rate, restructuring cash runs £50m to £100m a year above plan. The pension agreement also released permission, not cash: deficit payments continue at about £770m a year to FY30.

What would change my view. Service measures or Openreach repair times deteriorating as headcount falls; restructuring charges rising again; a second slip in the build.

Against the market. The market fully credits the cost programme and the TalkTalk purchase. The market credits the pension settlement in two ways, and one of them, pension cash falling from FY28, is wrong on the schedule in the company's own presentation. One positive has gone little noticed: in the same week, management raised the ambition of the labour target by about 10,000 roles.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. A broad, funded reset is largely delivered: new leadership as chief executive, as chief financial officer and at Openreach; the build peak passed on schedule, with capital expenditure falling by about a third; £1.7bn of a £3.5bn savings target done and labour down 11% with a tougher target; five disposals plus the Verizon joint venture; and two fresh tail-risk removals (TalkTalk bought for about £400m, and the pension settled early with distributions permitted). The reset repairs a mature business and lands in cash rather than in revenue or much EPS (6% to 7% a year), alongside weak first-half cash, Business EBITDA down 7%, a build slip and rising restructuring cost per leaver. The score therefore sits just below the group's 71 and below the levels' reset range of the low 60s to 75.

3Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management: sound foundations, not exceptional ones

Conclusion. BT has a favourable industry structure, a genuine cost moat and capable, operator-led management. Its financial profile is below average and improving, so BT's foundations are sound without being exceptional.

Evidence

  • Position. BT is number one in UK retail broadband (about 36% with TalkTalk), in small-business broadband and in mobile by revenue, and Openreach carries about 80% of UK broadband lines. UK mobile has three network operators.
  • Moat. Openreach passes a premise with fibre for about £300, against £500 to £1,800 for alternative networks. Fibre faults run at about a third of copper's. Openreach's network cannot be replicated economically at national scale.
  • Regulation cuts both ways. Ofcom's 'fair bet' lets Openreach earn above its cost of capital to 2031, with no cost-based price controls on 86% of premises. Open access and price caps limit how far BT can monetise the moat.
  • Financial profile against peers. BT's EBITDA margin of 47% matches KPN's, but below EBITDA BT lags its best peers on operating margin, capital intensity and returns (table below). Net debt of 2.6 times EBITDA on FactSet's basis is in line with peers; the pension is what sets BT's balance sheet apart. Adjusted EPS was two thirds above reported EPS in FY26.
  • Management. The chief executive has a record at Tele2, where total shareholder return was 52% against 6% for peers. The team is rebuilt for execution. Employee engagement has held at 76%, against a UK benchmark of 71%, through deep cuts, although the commercial culture lags the engineering culture. Bonuses are set on adjusted EBITDA and normalised free cash flow, the two measures that exclude pension and restructuring cash.

Inference. The industry structure is favourable, and Openreach's moat is real, physical and widening on cost. By regulatory design, however, the moat earns about the cost of capital, so it protects returns more than it creates excess returns. BT's financial profile is below average today and is improving mechanically as capital expenditure falls. Management is a strong operator with defensive goals: cash and margin on flat revenue.

So what. BT should be valued as a regulated infrastructure owner whose worth lies in its cash yield and in the distribution of that cash; a compounder's multiple does not apply. Within that frame, the improving cash conversion of BT's earnings (#6) is what can lift BT toward the better peers.
Counter-case. Success invites regulation. A retail share of 36%, falling line losses and rising Openreach returns (Bernstein sees them above 15% by about 2031) make intervention more likely, first through the CMA's review of the TalkTalk purchase and later through the post-2031 price review.

What would change my view. Return on capital employed failing to rise as capital expenditure falls; a CMA remedy that questions BT owning Openreach's two largest retail customers; evidence that top-tier speed, where alternative networks lead, starts to move mainstream customers.

Against the market. I agree with the market on the industry structure. I think the market underrates how much better KPN's economics are than BT's when it uses KPN as the precedent for a post-build re-rating: BT has the capital-expenditure cliff without KPN's returns or KPN's pension-free balance sheet.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. The industry structure is favourable (number one in a concentrated UK market, Openreach carrying about 80% of lines, and a network that cannot be replicated, built at about £300 a premise), and management is a capable operator. But the moat is regulated to about the cost of capital, so it protects rather than creates returns. The financial profile is below average (return on invested capital 3.2%, 24th percentile; capital expenditure 26% of revenue, 95th percentile; adjusted EPS two thirds above reported EPS; a pension plus 2.6 times leverage) and is improving only mechanically, with new fibre capital earning around its cost of capital. The score is coherent with the groups (72, 56, 33 and 60) and well below Tele2 (70), which earns a return on capital employed of 13%.

4Guidance: dependable, modestly conservative on operations, and never raised

Conclusion. BT's guidance is dependable and slightly conservative on EBITDA and line losses, has no buffer on cash, and comes from a management that meets but does not raise its guidance. Guidance therefore supports confidence in delivery and offers little scope for guidance-led upgrades.

Evidence

  • FY27 guidance, reconfirmed on 5 November 2026 and excluding TalkTalk: EBITDA of £8.1bn to £8.2bn; normalised free cash flow of about £2.0bn; Openreach line losses of about 800,000; and 'low-single-digit growth' in EPS. The mid-term guidance is revenue growth from FY28, capital expenditure more than £1bn below FY26, and about £3.0bn of normalised free cash flow by FY30.
  • Against the model. The model sits at the top of the EBITDA range, beats the line-loss guide by about 80,000 lines, and matches the cash guide in FY27, FY28 and FY30 with nothing to spare (table below).
  • Record. EBITDA has landed inside the guided range for three years. BT has met its cash floor for three years, but in FY26 only by £8m and with the help of £476m of factoring and supply-chain finance. Management cut the revenue outlook in November 2024. FY26 EBITDA reached 77% of the internal bonus target.
  • Behaviour. This management has not raised a profit or cash guide. In autumn 2026 Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telia, Telefonica and Vodafone all raised guidance, while BT only reconfirmed its guidance after a beat. Management's informal commentary runs above its formal guidance, and its tone toward short-sellers is combative.

Inference. BT's guidance is reliable and specific. The guidance is modestly conservative on operations and not conservative on cash. Nothing suggests a culture of keeping sell-side estimates low: where consensus sits below the company's targets (FY30 cash, FY28 revenue), the caution is the brokers' own.

So what. Expect delivery, and do not expect raises. Good news is more likely to take softer forms: a lower line-loss guide, the words 'top end', a higher cost-saving or labour ambition, or a capital-expenditure target met early. One quality flag for FY27: about 1.1p of EPS, more than the whole of the guided growth, comes from the end of amortisation of the intangible assets from the EE purchase, and that boost cannot repeat.
Counter-case. BT's guidance could prove conservative after all: the external forces improved after BT set the guidance, the second quarter beat by 3.2%, and Openreach's profit is growing 4%. A raise at the May results is possible; I put the chance of a raise at about one in five across the next 18 months.

What would change my view. A raised EBITDA or cash guide at any event. Alternatively, an FY27 cash figure that meets the guide only by redrawing the financing repaid in the first half, which would confirm the bears' view of BT's cash quality.

Against the market. Consensus FY27 EBITDA sits at the midpoint of guidance; I expect the top half. The market is sceptical of the FY30 cash ambition, with consensus at about £2.5bn against the £3.0bn target. I think the ambition is likely to be held, with a 15% chance each of it being brought forward or cut.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. EBITDA has landed inside the guided range three years running, and FY27 guidance is reconfirmed with core EBITDA tracking the top of the range. But no profit or cash guide has ever been raised, the revenue outlook was cut in November 2024, and the FY26 cash floor was met by only £8m with £476m of factoring and supply-chain finance. Guidance is therefore reliable and modestly conservative on EBITDA, but has no buffer on cash. The record is mixed, consistent with the Guidance (51) and Sell-side (46) groups.

5Does revenue growth lead to outsized profit growth? Yes, through fixed costs, but on small inputs and in both directions

Conclusion. BT's cost structure converts small revenue and EBITDA gains into EPS growth several times larger, through fixed depreciation and interest. The inputs are modest, and the same gearing works in reverse.

Evidence

  • The chain in the model, FY28 to FY30: revenue grows 0.9% a year, EBITDA 2.1%, operating profit 5.5% and EPS about 8%. Core EBITDA, excluding TalkTalk's swing from loss to profit, grows 1.3% a year.
  • Why the chain amplifies. Depreciation (about £4.7bn, larger than operating profit) and net finance cost (about £1.1bn) barely move, so small changes in EBITDA become large changes in EPS. One per cent of service revenue moves EPS by 4% to 6%, in either direction.
  • Pricing power is real at wholesale and nominal at retail. Openreach's revenue per line rose 7% from inflation indexation and fibre mix, and the model has that growth easing from 6% to 3%. Retail price rises of £4.00 a month on broadband stick with existing customers, yet measured broadband revenue per user fell, because discounts to new customers and the loss of voice revenue outweigh the price rises.
  • Cost savings reach profit only in part. £1.7bn of gross savings left EBITDA flat for three years. The model assumes that about a fifth of each year's £450m to £500m of savings reaches EBITDA from FY28, as the voice drag ends.
  • Feedback loops. Three loops reinforce growth: fibre take-up lowers faults and cost; each premise passed shrinks the room for overbuild and so reduces line losses; and falling capital expenditure funds deleveraging. Two loops balance growth: retail price elasticity, and a regulator whose reaction strengthens as BT does better.

Inference. The amplifier exists, and its inputs are small and mostly mechanical. Depreciation, BT's largest fixed cost, is the reason EPS grows faster than EBITDA. Because depreciation does not fall as the build ends, depreciation is also the reason EPS does not grow faster still.

So what. Each £100m of pre-tax profit is worth about 0.8p of EPS, about 4% of FY28 EPS. That gearing rewards the dependable 1% of EBITDA growth and punishes any shortfall equally.
Counter-case. Labour that BT capitalised into the build returns to operating cost as the build ends. BT capitalised about £2.2bn of labour in FY26, 48% of staff cost, and Redburn's ratio implies that up to £1bn could return to operating cost, erasing the whole EBITDA gain. The evidence so far is favourable: in the first half, capital expenditure fell 5%, labour fell 11% and EBITDA rose 1%. The harder test is the second half now under way, in which accrued capital expenditure must fall about 28%.

What would change my view. Openreach's EBITDA growth slowing from 4% as the build slows; own work capitalised, as reported in the June 2027 annual report, falling faster than headcount.

Against the market. The bulls expect savings from artificial intelligence to lift margins ahead of consensus, and depreciation to fall steeply. I agree on the direction of margins and disagree on depreciation, which the reported first half shows is still flat. The bears expect competition to absorb the savings; I think the end of the voice drag makes a 1% net EBITDA gain more likely than not.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. BT's structure has real gearing. Depreciation of about £4.7bn (larger than operating profit) and £1.1bn of interest are fixed, so 1% of service revenue moves EPS by 4% to 6%; Openreach takes and holds price rises linked to consumer-price inflation (+7% per line); financial leverage of 2.6 times amplifies EPS; and the scope for cost-out is large, with fibre lowering faults. The score sits below the levels' 75 because retail pricing is nominal, three years of £1.7bn of gross savings left EBITDA flat (only about a fifth is modelled to reach EBITDA), the input is only about 1% revenue growth, and the same gearing cuts as hard on the way down. It sits above the groups' 33 and 39 because those groups weigh returns and growth, not structure.

6Forecast financials: cash doubles by FY30, while adjusted EPS grows 6% to 7% a year

Conclusion. The forecasts show mid-to-high single-digit growth in adjusted EPS, double-digit growth in free cash flow and in reported earnings, and a balance sheet that deleverages by about 0.2 turns a year. That profile is clearly better than BT's past and falls short of a double-digit earnings story.

Evidence and inference

  • Every line grows faster than in the past. Revenue moves from about -1% a year to about +1%. Core EBITDA moves from flat to about +1% a year. Adjusted EPS moves from six flat years to growth of 6% to 7% a year. Normalised free cash flow, stuck at £1.3bn to £1.6bn for five years, doubles by FY30.
  • Double-digit growth appears in three places, and adjusted EPS is not one of them: normalised free cash flow (about 16% a year to FY30); shareholder cash, which rises more than fourfold; and reported EPS, which grows about 15% a year, from about 13.5p to about 22p, as restructuring and pension-interest charges shrink.
  • Margins rise less than before at the EBITDA level and more than before at the operating level. The EBITDA margin gains 0.1 to 0.2 points a year, against 1 to 2 points a year historically, because the easy gains from shedding low-margin units are done. The operating margin rises from 19.3% to 22.1%.
  • FY27 and FY28 EPS are both flattered and held back. The end of the EE amortisation adds about 1.1p in FY27 and 0.3p in FY28; TalkTalk takes off about 0.6p to 0.7p in each of those years.
So what. The right label for BT is an ex-growth business with a cash step-up, whose earnings quality is converging on its headline earnings. A reader who screens on adjusted EPS growth sees 6% to 7% a year. A reader who follows the shareholder's cash sees the dividend move from uncovered in FY27 (shareholder cash of £0.48bn against £0.83bn of dividends paid) to covered 2.3 times in FY30.
Counter-case. The earnings forecast leans on three things BT has not yet demonstrated: group EBITDA growth from savings, a TalkTalk turnaround worth about a fifth of the EPS gain to FY31, and revenue growth. UBS and Deutsche Bank forecast falling EBITDA, with FY29 figures of £7.7bn and £8.1bn against the model's £8.4bn.

What would change my view. FY28 guidance without revenue growth; an FY27 depreciation charge above £4.72bn; cash capital expenditure for FY28 guided above £4.0bn.

Against the market. On EPS I am with consensus and below the bulls: on my interpolation of its figures, most of the gap between the most bullish broker's FY29 EPS of 25.5p and the model's 20.7p is depreciation. On cash I am above consensus. On reported EPS, almost no one is looking.

Score: 48, set by the Rater. Growth of 0% to 5% gives a D, and the measure sits on the D/C boundary, so the score is placed at the top of the band. The growth is organic; FY27 is flat even with 1.1p from the end of the EE amortisation (TalkTalk dilutes FY27 and FY28); the operating margin rises from 19.3% to 22.1%, above anything in the record; and free cash flow and reported EPS grow in double digits. The score stays a D because adjusted EPS growth is well below the Universe's 11% median (consensus growth at the 18th percentile).

7Scope for upgrades over 6 to 12 months: moderate, back-loaded, and in cash rather than in EPS

Conclusion. Over the next six months, the balance of surprises is neutral for operations and slightly negative for EPS and for balance-sheet headlines. Over 6 to 18 months the balance turns favourable in cash. The scope for upgrades is therefore moderate and back-loaded.

Evidence: the sequence of news

Probabilities of revisions (the earlier Analyst's estimates, which I adopt)

The chart below gives each probability. The chance of a guidance cut or clear miss over the next 18 months (20% to 25%) rests almost entirely on FY27 cash.

Inference. The scope for upgrades is real, but it sits in the less-watched lines and arrives late. EBITDA estimates should edge up with good composition, as brokers raise Openreach, BT's highest-quality profit, and trim Consumer and Business. Cash estimates should rise as BT gives each capital-expenditure guide. Headline EPS, the line that revision screens count, is more likely to fall first, for presentational reasons.

So what. Revision screens will probably keep reading weak until mid-2027, even if operations run to plan. The first clean window for an upgrade cycle opens after the May results, when TalkTalk and the pension notes are in the numbers and FY28 guidance sets the base. For a stock that, in the words of the sector work, 'needs the cash itself', the cash revision is the one that matters, and cash is where the model is furthest above consensus.
Counter-case. Investors could mistake the presentational cuts for fundamental ones, and the cuts could then feed on themselves: a higher leverage headline, a lower EPS consensus and a split sell-side, in a sector the market is already selling.

What would change my view. Favourably: BT confirming that the interest on the pension notes sits outside adjusted earnings; an FY28 EBITDA guide with a midpoint above £8.25bn; TalkTalk cleared with a stated synergy figure. Unfavourably: an FY27 cash figure below £1.85bn; Consumer EBITDA falling; a required sale of TalkTalk's wholesale unit.

Against the market. The bulls expect upgrades through earnings; I expect upgrades through cash, and later. The bears expect cuts through competition; I expect the cuts that do come to stem largely from changes in perimeter and accounting. Neither side has framed the net-debt headline or the convergence of reported and adjusted earnings.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely met than moved (a raise about 20% likely, against 20% to 25% for a cut, mostly on FY27 cash). Consensus FY28 EPS is more likely trimmed than raised before May 2027 (50% down, against 15% up) as TalkTalk's losses, possible note interest and depreciation enter estimates, which on about 1% revenue growth is a large negative ratio. Against that, EBITDA estimates (50% likely up), FY29 and FY30 cash estimates (55% likely up) and the narrative should improve after the May results. The net is slightly negative and back-loaded, a little below the group's 42.

8Current momentum: weak in guidance, estimates and price, and weaker than peers on estimates

Conclusion. Momentum in guidance, estimates and price is weak for BT and mixed for its peers, so the case has no momentum support today.

Evidence

  • Guidance momentum is flat. BT has reconfirmed guidance twice in FY27, each time on a beat.
  • Sell-side momentum is negative. Consensus FY28 EPS is down 2% over one month and 3% over three months. The dashboard's revision score is -9, third from the bottom of 32 sector stocks, and its earnings-momentum rating is F (15 November 2026). Six of eleven visible brokers rate the shares Sell or Underweight. The median target price of 219p, barely above the share price, offers no pull.
  • Price momentum is rated D. The shares are 4.5% above a 200-day average that has risen in ten of the last twelve months, with returns of +22% over twelve months and -7% over six months. The shares peaked at 247.3p around the results and fell about 13% within days.
  • The narrative is fully articulated on both sides and entrenched. BT is one broker's 'best idea' and another's 'core Overweight', so among specialists the long case is well owned. The options market implies only a 14% chance that the shares trade above 270p within a year.
  • Peers are better on estimates and no better on price. Revision scores are +7 at Vodafone and +5 at KPN and Deutsche Telekom. Twenty-one of the 32 sector stocks are rated D or F on price momentum, and telecoms sit at the lowest grade of relative strength.

Inference. Momentum is weak on every measure, and BT's estimate momentum is weak even against a sector whose own estimate momentum is unremarkable. The price behaviour suggests that holders treat the de-risking as known and are waiting for delivery.

So what. Nothing in current momentum supports the multiple. The stock is trading on fundamentals not yet reported, in a sector the market is selling as leveraged and long-duration.
Counter-case. Weak momentum combined with improving fundamentals is where turns begin. Hedge-fund positioning was lighter by mid-2026 than a year before, and about 41% of the share register sits in three strategic hands, so a clean cash print could move a thin free float sharply.

What would change my view. Revisions to EBITDA and cash estimates turning positive after February; the shares holding the 200-day average through the presentational negatives; falling bond yields.

Against the market. I have no disagreement with the market here: the dashboard's letter grades describe BT's momentum accurately.

Score: 30, set by the Rater. Both momentum measures are negative, but relative strength is not in the bottom fifth (the price is 4.5% above a rising 200-day average and up 22% over twelve months), so the grade is D. The score is placed in the lower half of the band because consensus FY28 EPS has been cut over one and three months, six of eleven brokers rate the shares Sell, guidance was only reconfirmed on a beat, the shares fell 13% after the results, and peers' estimate momentum is better than BT's.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts: a low-risk business, but not a low-risk case at this price

Conclusion. BT's forecasts are simple, trackable and narrow, but the share price is exposed to sudden moves in a multiple that is high in its own range and geared to bond yields. The business is low risk; the case at this price is not.

Simplicity. The forecast has one cause, the end of the build, which is physical and in management's hands. No single external driver moves FY28 EPS by more than about 2%. The plausible range is about ±2% for FY28 EBITDA, ±8% for FY28 EPS (roughly 17.5p to 20.7p) and ±10% for free cash flow. The range is skewed mildly to the downside, because management does not exceed its guides and the items not yet in anyone's numbers are mostly costs.

The five judgements, with the arithmetic. One rule of thumb applies to all five: £100m of pre-tax profit, less 23% tax, spread over about 9.9bn shares, is about 0.8p of EPS.

1. The second half of FY27 delivers the cash, and capital expenditure keeps falling.

  • The need. BT needs about £1.76bn of normalised free cash flow in the second half, against £0.94bn a year earlier, to reach about £2.0bn for the year.
  • The build-up. Second-half EBITDA of about £4.05bn, less about £0.88bn of leases, cash interest and cash tax, leaves about £3.2bn. Less cash capital expenditure of £1.83bn (the model's £4.35bn for the year, less £2.52bn already spent) leaves about £1.35bn. Working capital must then return about £0.4bn, after absorbing £0.47bn in the first half.
  • If the judgement is wrong. With cash capital expenditure of £2.05bn (Morgan Stanley's figure) and the same working capital, the half delivers £1.55bn and the year £1.78bn. EPS is unaffected, and net debt is £0.2bn higher, 0.02 turns of EBITDA. The damage is to investors' belief in the FY30 cash target.
  • If capital expenditure then runs £300m a year above plan from FY28 to FY30 (Deutsche Bank's case that savings must be spent on faster fibre technology, mobile and harder-to-reach premises), FY30 free cash flow is £2.75bn, short of the £3.0bn target. Net debt is £0.9bn higher, at 2.27 times EBITDA in place of 2.16 times. Extra interest of about £45m and extra depreciation of about £50m take about 0.7p (3%) off FY30 EPS, and the first buyback slips beyond FY31.

2. Core EBITDA grows about 1% a year from FY28.

  • Base. The model's core EBITDA is £8,190m, £8,272m, £8,379m and £8,488m for FY27 to FY30.
  • If core EBITDA is flat, the shortfall is £82m, £189m and £298m in FY28 to FY30. EPS falls by 0.6p, 1.5p and 2.3p, to about 18.5p, 19.2p and 19.9p, and EPS growth drops from about 7% a year to under 3%. FY30 free cash flow is £2.76bn and leverage 2.3 times.
  • If core EBITDA grows 2% a year, EBITDA is £82m, £142m and £203m higher; EPS gains 0.6p, 1.1p and 1.6p, reaching about 23.8p in FY30; and free cash flow reaches about £3.26bn.
  • The swing factor is capitalised labour (#5). Each £100m of labour cost that returns to operating cost without a matching fall in headcount costs 0.8p of EPS.

3. Depreciation stays near £4.7bn, and the interest on the pension notes stays outside adjusted earnings.

  • The notes. The pension notes are borrowings of BT Finance plc, issued on 13 November 2026. The research reads BT's documents, with medium confidence, as placing the notes inside reported net debt. The notes accrue interest of about £85m to £120m in FY28, and BT has not said whether that interest sits inside adjusted earnings.
  • If the note interest is inside adjusted earnings, it takes 0.7p to 0.9p off FY28 EPS, 0.5p off FY29 and 0.3p off FY30. If depreciation is also £60m higher (0.5p), FY28 EPS is about 18.0p, below FY27, and BT loses its guide of EPS 'growth'.
  • If depreciation falls as an earlier stage of this analysis assumed (£30m, £90m and £150m lower in FY28 to FY30), EPS gains 0.2p, 0.7p and 1.2p. A larger write-off of copper assets after the switch-off is the unevidenced upside; the fixed-asset note in the June 2027 annual report will show whether that write-off exists.

4. Openreach's line losses keep falling.

  • Base. The model's line losses are 720,000, 550,000, 480,000 and 450,000 for FY27 to FY30. Each 100,000 lines is worth about £21m of revenue and £19m of EBITDA a year, about 0.15p of EPS.
  • If losses stay at 800,000 a year, a cumulative 1.0m more lines are gone by FY30. That costs about £190m of EBITDA, 1.5p (7%) of FY30 EPS and about £210m (3%) of Openreach revenue. In FY28 alone the effect is only about 0.3p.
  • If Sky moves the 450,000 to 650,000 lines that Redburn identifies, the cost is £85m to £125m of EBITDA, or 0.7p to 1.0p of EPS.
  • Line losses are small in any one quarter and large in the narrative, because they are the published gauge of Openreach's moat.

5. TalkTalk is cleared on behavioural terms and turns from loss to profit.

  • Base. The model's TalkTalk EBITDA is -£50m, -£40m, +£40m, +£100m and +£130m for FY27 to FY31.
  • If BT keeps TalkTalk and TalkTalk still loses £60m a year, FY30 EBITDA is £160m lower, costing 1.25p (6%) of EPS.
  • If the CMA requires a sale of TalkTalk's wholesale unit (about 30% likely), the cost is £20m to £40m of FY29 EBITDA, or 0.15p to 0.3p, and about 1.0m wholesale lines become free to move, each 100,000 worth 0.15p.
  • If the purchase is unwound (within the 15% tail), TalkTalk's losses go, adding 0.3p in FY28; its FY30 profit goes, costing 0.8p; and the original risk returns: about 2.7m lines carrying about £1bn of Openreach revenue.
  • Whatever the outcome, TalkTalk entering estimates will read as a cut of about 3.5% to FY28 EPS.

Summary of the five judgements (effect on EPS in pence, adverse case; my arithmetic)

The five judgements are largely independent, which narrows the combined range. The first two share one root, however: if labour does not leave as the build ends, both capitalised cost and operating cost stay high.

Trackability. BT publishes every operating driver each quarter: line losses, revenue per line, take-up, divisional EBITDA, labour, capital expenditure and net debt. The gaps are below EBITDA. Depreciation, interest and EPS appear only half-yearly, BT never gives the bridge from gross savings to EBITDA, and the three accounting questions (the pension notes, their interest and TalkTalk) will not be visible before May 2027. The case can therefore be tracked well for whether it is on plan, and poorly for whether EPS is running ahead of or behind estimates.

Sudden risks. Each fundamental sudden risk looks possible rather than probable: a CMA remedy on TalkTalk; a gilt shock reaching the pension through collateral calls; a large wholesale defection; a failed switch-off of the old telephone network, with about 1m lines still to migrate before 31 January; and a cyber attack or network outage. The sentiment risks are larger at this price: a further rise in yields; a block sale by Bharti (24.95%) or Deutsche Telekom (12.06%); and sector narratives about switching agents built on artificial intelligence and about satellite broadband.

Precedents

  • BT's own multiple has moved 1.5 to 3 turns within one to four months, three times in four years: from 9.4 to 6.2 times between June and September 2022 in the gilt crisis, with the shares down 35%; from 12.3 to 10.5 times within a month in 2025; and from 13.2 to 10.1 times between February and June 2026.
  • The sector de-rated 12% in mid-2026 with estimates unchanged. A leveraged defensive stock de-rates first when yields rise, and with equity at about half of BT's enterprise value, a 5% fall in enterprise value is about a 10% fall in equity value.
  • Post-build peers (KPN, Chorus) did deliver the cash, which supports the central forecast. Chorus's depreciation fell only when Chorus wrote off copper, and then by under 10%, which supports the sticky depreciation path in the model.
  • Vodafone Germany lost about a fifth of its profit in three years as cable volumes left a fixed-cost network. Falling line losses keep Openreach away from that path.
  • BT's cyclicality is low. In the 2022 to 2024 inflation shock, BT held EBITDA through pricing and cost.
Counter-case to my reading. The risk may be lower than the price suggests, because the tail risks that kept BT's multiple low for a decade (the pension, dividend cover and a funded challenger) are the ones that have just receded.

What would change my view. A clean FY27 cash print; clearance of the TalkTalk purchase; BT presenting leverage and note interest in a way that removes the accounting ambiguity.

Against the market. The bears locate the risk in competition; I locate most of it in the multiple and in presentation. The bulls treat the forecast as low risk, which I accept for cash and not for the EPS path the bulls publish.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. The operating case is simple and trackable: one cause (the end of the build); FY28 EBITDA within about ±2% and FY28 EPS within about ±8% (17.5p to 20.7p), skewed mildly down; low cyclicality; and quarterly disclosure of every operating driver. Against that, several features make the share-price outcome much wider: the gearing below EBITDA; leverage of 2.6 to 2.8 times plus a pension and the pension notes; three accounting questions not visible before May 2027; a two-sided second-half cash print and CMA review; and a multiple at the 82nd percentile that has moved 1.5 to 3 turns within months three times in four years, with equity at about half of enterprise value. The score sits between the Risks groups (38 and 63).

10Lifecycle: a stalling stock on a business that is turning up

Conclusion. BT is a stalling stock on a business that is turning up. BT has a dated chance to move to the reinforcing phase from May 2027, and a smaller chance of breaking down if the cash print disappoints while yields rise.

Evidence

  • Fundamentals are turning up. The capital cycle has turned, line losses are falling, BT has reported its first revenue growth in two and a half years, and the cash inflection is due in the half now under way.
  • The thesis has already broadened. The shares have doubled from about 105p in April 2024, and the multiple rose from under 6 times to a peak of 13.2 times in February 2026. The long case is a specialist favourite.
  • Momentum has stalled (#8), upgrades are scarce (#7), and the shares fell on good news.
  • The Master Dashboard's rule gives a starting phase of Bottoming (23 November 2026).

Inference. I read BT as a stock stalling after a re-rating, in a business that is turning up. The Bottoming phase normally describes a washed-out multiple and deeply cut estimates, and BT has neither: its multiple is at the 82nd percentile, and estimates have been trimmed by only 2% to 3%. The dashboard's label fits the momentum readings and not the valuation. The practical consequence of the disagreement is small, because Viewforth's guideline assigns a low-in-range multiple to the stalling and bottoming phases alike.

So what. A stalled stock needs new evidence to move to the reinforcing phase, and for BT that evidence is dated: the FY27 cash print and FY28 guidance on 13 May 2027, then the first half of FY28 in November 2027. My probabilities for the next twelve months are: moves to reinforcing, about 35%; stays stalled, about 45%; breaks down, about 20%. A breakdown needs a cash miss or a further rise in yields, and most likely both.
Counter-case. The stall could be the pause before a second leg up. If the cash arrives as planned, a stock with a 4% dividend yield and normalised free cash flow worth 9% to 13% of its market value each year does not stay stalled for long.

What would change my view. Toward reinforcing: the favourable signposts in #7. Toward breaking down: an FY27 cash print below £1.85bn together with line losses above 200,000 a quarter.

Against the market. The bullish brokers already place BT in the reinforcing phase. The price action since the results on 5 November disagrees with them, and so do I.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's 'stalling after a re-rating' rather than the computed Bottoming: the multiple has doubled to the 82nd percentile of its range, estimates are only trimmed, momentum has stalled and the shares fell on a beat, while the business underneath is turning up (the capital-expenditure cycle has turned, line losses are falling and the cash inflection is due). A dated route to Reinforcing (about 35% likely in twelve months) lifts the score slightly above a plain stall.

11The fair multiple: about 9 times, between the guideline's 7.25 times and today's 10.9 to 11.4 times

Conclusion. The guideline's 7.25 times is a prudent floor. I place fair value at about 9 times, within a range of 8.5 to 10 times: above the guideline because BT's earnings are becoming cash, and below today's multiple because that cash is not yet being paid out.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline sets the fair multiple for a stock in the Bottoming phase at 7.25 times two-year-forward earnings, the 30th percentile of BT's ten-year history. The guideline multiple is 37% below the 11.4 times the dashboard shows now, and topic #12 uses it.

Evidence

  • The ten-year range runs from 6.0 times at the 10th percentile, through 8.3 times at the median and 9.9 times at the 75th percentile, to 11.6 times at the 90th. The market has rarely held BT above 11 times.
  • What that history contains: an accounting scandal, a dividend suspended and then halved, a build that took capital expenditure from £4.1bn to £5.2bn, and a pension deficit in the billions. Throughout that history, a pound of adjusted earnings delivered only 20p to 30p of cash to the shareholder.
  • Two valuation anchors disagree today (second chart below). On dividend yield BT is expensive: its 4.0% yield is below both the ten-year gilt and the sector, and only at the guideline price of about 160p does the FY28 dividend yield (5.5%) approach the sector's. On cash yield BT looks inexpensive: normalised free cash flow is 9% of market value in FY27 and nearly 13% in FY29.
  • Against peers. BT trades at 10.6 times current earnings, against a sector median of about 12.4 times. At today's enterprise value, BT stands on about 14 times FY27 operating free cash flow and about 11 times FY29's, against a peer average of 12.7 times and KPN's 15.8 times on 2026 figures (my arithmetic; definitions are not matched). On that measure the price credits about a third of the improvement in operating free cash flow due by FY29.

Inference. The guideline is the right kind of multiple for a stock whose forecasts are uncertain. BT's forecasts are unusually certain, and the cash behind each pound of BT's earnings is rising from about a quarter of a pound to about one pound. Both facts argue that 7.25 times is too low as a central estimate. My fair range is 8.5 to 10 times, centred near 9 times: the ten-year median plus about one turn for earnings that are becoming cash. I would not go higher, for four reasons: EPS grows 6% to 7% a year, not in double digits; equity is half of enterprise value; the dividend yield is below the gilt yield; and the cash does not become distributions until about FY31.

So what. The gap between the two anchors closes only when BT pays the cash out. Until then the market must take the cash on trust, which makes BT a long-duration claim and explains its sensitivity to gilt yields. The guideline's 7.25 times is roughly what BT is worth if the market values it on dividend yield alone. Today's multiple is roughly what BT is worth if the market credits the cash in full. My 9 times sits between the two and is close to the multiple at which the 18-month return is nil.
Counter-case. Higher: the tail risks that defined BT's history have receded, and infrastructure buyers pay more than 11 times earnings for regulated cash. Lower: the guideline could prove right if yields rise further or the cash print fails, and the precedents in #9 show that BT's multiple can fall that far within months.

What would change my view. Up: a buyback brought forward; ten-year gilt yields below 4.5%; two clean years of cash delivery. Down: note interest and TalkTalk taking FY28 EPS below FY27; a rating agency reacting against the leverage headline.

Against the market. The market pays 10.9 to 11.4 times. I think that multiple prices a clean delivery and a benign path for yields, and leaves little margin for the presentational negatives of the next six months.

Score: 33, set by the Rater. Dear on one measure and neutral on the other gives a D. The score is placed in the lower middle of the band: the memo's own fair multiple of about 9 times (range 8.5 to 10 times) sits well below today's 10.9 to 11.4 times; the stalling phase deserves a lower-in-range multiple; and BT has historically traded below peers, so the discount to peers flatters it. Only the rising cash conversion of BT's earnings argues that the history understates fair value.

12Total shareholder return: negative at the guideline multiple, near zero at fair value, and decided by the multiple

Conclusion. At the guideline multiple, the model's return is -18.5% to March 2028 and -7.0% to September 2029. A one-third fall in the multiple drives both figures and outweighs dependable earnings growth and dividends worth about 11 to 13 points a year. The return therefore depends on which multiple the market pays for cash that BT does not yet distribute.

The model's return at the guideline multiple (price 215p on 16 November 2026; multiple 10.9 times today and 7.25 times at the guideline)

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedFrom earningsFrom the multipleFrom dividendsValue per share
To 31 March 2028-18.5%-14.0%+12.1%-33.5%+6.9%176p
To 30 September 2029-7.0%-2.5%+23.0%-33.5%+11.2%200p

How the terms combine. The earnings and multiple terms multiply, and dividends add. To March 2028, 1.121 times 0.665 gives 0.745: a price fall of about 25%, to about 160p, plus dividends of about 15p. No other cash returns fall inside either horizon, because buybacks beyond employee share plans start only in FY31 in the model.

What drives each term

  • Earnings (+12% and +23%). The two-year-forward EPS rolls from about 19.7p today to about 22.1p (FY30) at the first horizon and about 24.3p at the second. Earnings are the dependable term: the whole plausible range of the forecast is worth about 8 points of return.
  • Dividends (+7% and +11%). The dividends are near-certain, although shareholder cash does not cover them until FY28.
  • The multiple (-33.5%). The fall in the multiple is the entire reason the return is negative. At the first horizon, each turn of the multiple is worth about 22p of share price, or about 10 points of return.

The same return at other multiples (my arithmetic on the model's terms)

Multiple at the horizonTo 31 March 2028 (annualised)To 30 September 2029 (annualised)
7.25x, the guideline-18.5% (-14.0%)-7.0% (-2.5%)
8.3x, the ten-year median-8% (-6%)+5% (+2%)
9.1xabout nil+14% (+5%)
9.9x, the 75th percentile+9% (+6%)+23% (+7%)

Inference

  • Time works for the holder at about 11 to 13 points a year. Earnings growth plus dividends offset a fall in the multiple of 11% to 13% a year. Over three years the return is positive at any multiple above about 7.9 times.
  • A cross-check supports the unchanged-multiple case. From FY28 BT retires about 11p to 18p a share of debt and pension obligation each year, 5% to 8% of today's price, on top of the 4% dividend and about 1% of EBITDA growth geared twice. That sum gives 11% to 14% a year at an unchanged enterprise-value multiple, consistent with the 11% to 13% from the earnings route.
  • Over six months the return is almost wholly the multiple. Dividends add about 1% and the earnings roll-forward about 3%.
  • At my fair range of 8.5 to 10 times, the return is about -6% to +10% to March 2028 and about +7% to +24% to September 2029.
So what: the skew. In my judgement, the multiple at March 2028 has about a 35% probability of being at or above 9.9 times, about 40% of being between 8.3 and 9.9 times, and about 25% of being below 8.3 times. That distribution gives a roughly symmetric 18-month outcome centred near zero, and a positive three-year outcome in all but the lowest quarter of outcomes. The model's -18.5% describes the lower end of the distribution.
Counter-case. If the market values BT as a plain yield stock at the sector's dividend yield, the guideline's return becomes the central case.

What would change my view. The signposts are those in #7 and #11; the first to watch is the FY27 cash print.

Against the market. The median broker target of 219p implies that the multiple holds. The guideline implies that the multiple loses a third. I sit between the two: nearer the median broker over three years, and undecided over eighteen months.

Score: 27, set by the Rater. A return of about nil to a few percent gives a D at its floor (nil maps to about 25). The score is lifted a little because the three-year check is positive in all but the lowest quarter of outcomes, and dividends plus earnings add 11 to 13 points a year. It is held near the floor because the lower tail is fat: the model's own -18.5%, and precedents of the multiple losing 3 turns within months in a sector being sold on yields.

13Summary conclusion: a better, more predictable business whose improvement the price already reflects

BT is a better business than it was three months ago, and a more predictable one than most. The build is ending, the cash is coming, the challengers are short of capital, TalkTalk (the source of more than half of Openreach's line losses) is inside the group, and the pension is settled. Management has shown that it will act to remove risks and will deliver what it guides.

Three things keep BT from being the kind of situation Richard looks for today.

  1. The improvement reaches cash long before it reaches EPS, and the model's EPS forecast sits on consensus.
  2. The next six months bring headlines that read badly (higher reported net debt, TalkTalk dilution, no buyback) around one genuinely uncertain figure, the second-half cash.
  3. The market has already paid for the de-risking: the multiple is high in its own range, momentum is weak and the sector is being sold on yields.
What would make BT that kind of situation is specific and dated. A clean FY27 cash print on 13 May 2027, FY28 guidance with revenue growth and capital expenditure below £3.9bn, and settled accounting questions would open a window in which cash estimates rise, reported net debt falls by more than £1bn a year and the earnings behind each share become cash. A lower multiple before then would improve the odds further. Five measures will show whether that window opens.
Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 60, set by the Rater. The input forces are clearly positive (tailwinds 59, a broad internal reset 68) and reliably reach cash, doubling normalised free cash flow by FY30. But they reach forecast profits only weakly, with adjusted EPS up about 5% to 7% a year (topic 6, a D at 48), below the Universe median. Per the levels, clearly positive inputs that lift profits to about median growth sit in the low to mid 60s, so this score sits just below that range, under the memo's B.
Foundations' Robustness: 62, set by the Rater. Quality is middling (topic 3 at 56), because returns sit near the cost of capital and the balance sheet carries leverage and a pension, and delivery is reliable but never raised (topic 4 at 50). Following Richard's reasoning on CVS, stability lifts the score above both topics: a near-monopoly wholesale network in a concentrated market, non-discretionary demand, wholesale pricing linked to consumer-price inflation, and EBITDA held through the inflation shock. Stability does not lift the score as far as CVS's 80, given the leverage, the pension and the regulatory cap on returns.
Setups' Fit/Crispness: 60, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits a major Cause-for-Concern Clearing in a business of middling quality (pension settled, wholesale threat eased, capital-expenditure cliff passed, TalkTalk inside the group), which Richard places at 65 to 75, and it half-fits a Big Corporate Change-driven EPS upgrade setup. The score is held below that range because today's problems blur the setup (weak first-half cash, Business EBITDA down 7%, falling retail revenue per user) and because the step-up lands in cash rather than in EPS. The memo's objection that the concerns cleared at a high multiple is a point about price, and is left to topics 11 and 12.
Case Riskiness: 48, set by the Rater. The operating case is simple and narrow (topic 9 at 50). Unlike Richard's Arteche case at 60, where the main risk was only a high multiple, BT adds 2.6 to 2.8 times leverage plus a pension, with equity at about half of enterprise value, three accounting changes by May 2027 and a two-sided cash print. A multiple at the 82nd percentile and geared to gilt yields is therefore amplified in the equity. The result is a moderate-risk case, a little below the middle.

  • Forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2). I have changed no forecast input. Earnings per share (EPS) are BT's adjusted basic figure, the basis brokers use (18.3p in FY26). The model's summary prints EPS to the nearest penny; the tenths of a penny quoted here are derived from its growth rates.
  • FY27 EPS growth. The model's summary shows FY27 EPS growth of +5.1%, measured against a different historical definition of FY26 EPS (17.5p). On the brokers' basis, FY27 EPS is flat.
  • Group includes TalkTalk from 5 October 2026, as the model does. Core excludes TalkTalk, as company guidance and consensus do.
  • Three cash measures appear. Normalised free cash flow is the company's guided measure: cash flow after capital expenditure, leases, interest paid and tax paid, and before pension deficit payments, restructuring and spectrum. Shareholder cash is normalised free cash flow less those three items, before dividends. The model's 'equity free cash flow' deducts the tax and interest charged to profit in place of the amounts paid, so it reads £0.5bn to £0.6bn a year lower than normalised free cash flow. That gap is one of definition; no forecast differs.
  • Leverage uses the earlier Analyst's net-debt bridge, because the model's net-debt line leaves out pension cash, restructuring cash and the pension notes. The cash and net-debt lines of the forecast table in #6 come from the same bridge.
  • Probabilities of guidance changes and revisions in #7 are the earlier Analyst's, which I adopt.
  • The multiple is the two-year-forward price-to-earnings ratio: 10.9 times on the model's earnings and 11.3 to 11.4 times on consensus.
  • Abbreviations in charts and tables. CMA is the Competition and Markets Authority; capex is capital expenditure; FCF is free cash flow; ROCE and ROIC are return on capital employed and return on invested capital; VMO2 is Virgin Media O2; DT is Deutsche Telekom; H1 and H2 are the first and second halves of the fiscal year.
  • Latest results. The latest Earnings Review covers the half to 30 September 2026, reported on 5 November 2026; I checked its revenue (£8,750m) and EBITDA (£4,097m) against FactSet's latest period, and they match.

Charts marked as drawn for this memo take their figures from the memo text; the default charts and the five financial tables come from FactSet and the Financial Analyst's model (update 2), as each note says. Grades are from the Rater's scores.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
